## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.rival.0)

BODY
No prior account is available to build on — the selected previous view is absent — so this begins from the asker's description alone, which is itself worth flagging: everything below inherits one participant's angle on a three-person situation.

Three features of the description seem to do most of the explanatory work, and they are not one problem.

First, the disputes are about what an agreement meant, not about whether a task was done. That points at underspecification rather than bad faith: an agreement like 'you take the bins' leaves frequency, standard and deadline open, and each person later reads the gap in their own favor. If that is right, more argument about the past is the wrong tool; what is missing is a way of fixing terms at the moment an agreement is made.

Second, the schedules change, so any fixed split decays. An allocation that was fair in March is unfair by May without anyone misbehaving. A one-time settlement cannot hold; what is needed is a renewal mechanism — which suggests a short, boring, calendarised check-in rather than episodic negotiations that each carry the full weight of accumulated grievance.

Third, the friend who has started avoiding the conversations is the least knowable part and probably the most important. Avoidance of a recurring conversation is usually maintained by the conversation being aversive, and a conversation dominated by retrospective dispute is predictably aversive. There is also a structural suspect: in a three-person household, a group conversation about chores can take on a two-on-one character for whichever resident is least aligned with the other two, so that it feels like judgment rather than planning. But two opposite explanations of the avoidance fit the material — the friend feels unfairly blamed or outnumbered, or the friend is dodging obligations they know they are not meeting — and these call for different responses. The asker cannot tell them apart from inside their own framing, and neither can this account.

One caution the account should carry: it is entirely consistent with the description that the friends experience the asker as relitigating past agreements with prosecutorial energy, and that the avoidance is partly a response to that. The first test of any remedy is whether it survives asking the other two what they think the problem is.

With that in place, what seems worth conjecturing, in decreasing order of confidence:

1. Doer-worded written agreements. When someone agrees to a task, they write down in a shared note or group chat what they agreed to, in their own words, with a frequency or deadline. The doer's own words matter: it is much harder to later dispute the meaning of a sentence you wrote yourself. The asker can start unilaterally with their own undertakings.

2. A recurring short check-in — fifteen minutes, fortnightly — with a fixed agenda: what did not work since last time, and what needs adjusting given the coming period's schedules. Its function is to move disputes off the trigger path: an argument about the bins at the moment the bins are full becomes a scheduled item instead, and schedule drift gets a standing venue.

3. One-on-one, low-stakes contact with the avoiding friend, framed as a question — what would make this easier for you? — rather than as a summons back into the group conversation. Forcing the group format on someone already avoiding it is likely to deepen the avoidance, and it forfeits the chance to learn which explanation of the avoidance is true.

4. A limit rather than a recommendation: how far to formalize (rotas, standards, apps) is constrained by the fact that these are friends. Some explicitness reduces friction; past some point it reads as contract enforcement between friends. Where that line sits is household-specific and will have to be found by trying the light measures first and watching how they land.

The order of operations matters: reduce the aversiveness and ambiguity of coordination first, then ask what the avoider actually needs. The chore disputes look tractable with format changes; the avoidance does not, because its causes are so far only conjectured.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
